+Custom representation formats may also be registered into the Astropy Cosmology
+I/O framework for use by these methods. For details of the framework see
+:ref:`io_registry`.

+.. EXAMPLE START : custom to/from format
+
+As an example, the following is an implementation of an `astropy.table.Row`
+converter. Note that we can use other registered parsers -- here "mapping"
+-- to make the implementation much simpler.

+We start by defining the function to parse a `astropy.table.Row` into a
+`~astropy.cosmology.Cosmology`. This function should take 1 positional
+argument, the row object, and 2 keyword arguments, for how to handle
+extra metadata and which Cosmology class to use. Details about metadata
+treatment are in ``Cosmology.from_format.help("mapping")``.

+.. code-block:: python
+    :emphasize-lines: 12,13

+    >>> import copy
+    >>> from astropy.cosmology import Cosmology
+    
+    >>> def from_table_row(row, *, move_to_meta=False, cosmology=None):

+    ...     name = row['name'] if 'name' in row.columns else None
+    ...     meta = copy.deepcopy(row.meta)
+    ...     # turn row into mapping (dict of the arguments)
+    ...     mapping = dict(row)
+    ...     mapping["meta"] = meta
+    ...     # build cosmology from map
+    ...     return Cosmology.from_format(mapping,
+    ...                                  move_to_meta=move_to_meta, cosmology=cosmology)

+`~astropy.cosmology.Cosmology` into a `~astropy.table.Row`. This function
+requires only the cosmology object and a ``*args`` to absorb unneeded
+information passed by `astropy.io.registry.UnifiedReadWrite` (which
+implements `astropy.cosmology.Cosmology.to_format`).
+
+.. code-block:: python
+    :emphasize-lines: 4

+    
+    >>> def to_table_row(cosmology, *args):
+    ...     p = cosmology.to_format("mapping")
+    ...     p["cosmology"] = p["cosmology"].__qualname__  # as string
+    ...     meta = p.pop("meta")
+    ...     # package parameters into lists for Table parsing
+    ...     params = {k: [v] for k, v in p.items()}
+    ...     return QTable(params, meta=meta)[0]  # return row
+
+Last we write a function to help with format auto-identification and then
+register everything into `astropy.io.registry`.
+
+.. code-block:: python
+    :emphasize-lines: 11, 12, 13
+
+    >>> from astropy.cosmology import Cosmology
+    >>> from astropy.io import registry as io_registry
+    >>> from astropy.table import Row
+
+    >>> def row_identify(origin, format, *args, **kwargs):
+    ...     """Identify if object uses the Table format."""
+    ...     if origin == "read":
+    ...         return isinstance(args[1], Row) and (format in (None, "row"))
+    ...     return False
+
+    >>> io_registry.register_reader("row", Cosmology, from_table_row)
+    >>> io_registry.register_writer("row", Cosmology, to_table_row)
+    >>> io_registry.register_identifier("row", Cosmology, row_identify)
+

+:meth:`astropy.cosmology.Cosmology.from_format` and
+:meth:`astropy.cosmology.Cosmology.to_format`.
+
+.. code-block:: python
+
+    >>> from astropy.cosmology import Planck18
+    >>> row = Planck18.to_format("row")
+    >>> row
+    <Row index=0>
+      cosmology     name        H0        Om0    Tcmb0    Neff    m_nu [3]    Ob0  
+                           km / (Mpc s)                              eV            
+        str13       str8     float64    float64 float64 float64   float64   float64
+    ------------- -------- ------------ ------- ------- ------- ----------- -------
+    FlatLambdaCDM Planck18        67.66 0.30966  2.7255   3.046 0.0 .. 0.06 0.04897

+    ...     pass
+
+.. EXAMPLE END

 Overview
 ========
 
+.. _whatsnew-5.0-cosmology:
+
+Support for reading, writing, and converting ``Cosmology``
+==========================================================
+
+Four new methods -- ``read``, ``write``, ``to_format``, ``from_format`` -- have
+been added to the ``Cosmology`` class, enabling reading from and writing to
+files and converting between different python objects.
+The methods use Astropy's Unified I/O registry so custom formats can be
+registered. Details are discussed in an addition to the docs.
+
+Currently no file formats are registered, but the syntax is as follows:
+
+.. doctest-skip::
+
+    >>> from astropy.cosmology import Planck18
+    >>> Planck18.write('<file name>.<format>')
+    >>>
+    >>> from astropy.cosmology import Cosmology
+    >>> cosmo = Cosmology.read('<file name>.<format>')
+    >>> cosmo == Planck18
+    True
+
+
+The transformation between ``Cosmology`` and `dict` is pre-registered,
+e.g. enabling::
+
+    >>> from astropy.cosmology import Planck18
+    >>> cm = Planck18.to_format("mapping")
+    >>> cm
+    {'cosmology': <class 'astropy.cosmology.core.FlatLambdaCDM'>,
+     'name': 'Planck18',
+     'H0': <Quantity 67.66 km / (Mpc s)>,
+     'Om0': 0.30966,
+     ...
+
+    >>> from astropy.cosmology import Cosmology
+    >>> cosmo = Cosmology.from_format(cm, format="mapping")
+    >>> cosmo == Planck18
+    True
+

+To ensure consistent use of a prior version of constants in other Astropy

### `Beeswarm` (class) — `seaborn/categorical.py`
> A class that algorithmically repositions scatter plot points to avoid overlaps in a beeswarm visualization pattern.
The Beeswarm class implements collision detection and spatial repositioning logic for categorical scatter plots, determining which points could overlap based on their radii, generating candidate positions around neighbors, and selecting the first non-overlapping placement. It handles both vertical and horizontal orientations, applies width constraints via gutter boundaries, and is designed to be applied at draw time to ensure robustness against axis limit and layout changes. The class provides methods to detect overlapping circles, generate offset candidates at specific distances, filter candidates for non-collision, and apply boundary constraints, enabling dynamic point arrangement that adapts to the most recent figure state.
- `beeswarm`: `beeswarm(self, orig_xyr)`
  > Adjusts x-coordinates of points to prevent overlaps while preserving their y-positions and radii.
  The method takes a sorted array of points with x, y, and radius columns (orig_xyr) and repositions them along the categorical axis to avoid overlaps while maintaining their value-axis order. It operates in point coordinates where x is always the categorical axis, handling both vertical and horizontal orientations through coordinate transformations. The algorithm ensures that the minimum distance between any two points equals or exceeds their combined radii, as verified by test assertions checking pairwise distances. The method is called after points are sorted by their value-axis coordinate to facilitate efficient overlap detection and resolution.
- `could_overlap`: `could_overlap(self, xyr_i, swarm)`
  > Identifies swarm points that could spatially overlap with a target point based on distance and radius.
  This method filters a sorted list of swarm points to return only those whose circles (defined by position and radius) could potentially overlap with a target point's circle. The method takes a target point represented as (x, y, radius) and a list of existing swarm points in the same format, using geometric distance calculations to determine overlap candidates. The implementation works backwards through the swarm list and can short-circuit for efficiency rather than using vectorized operations. The removal of the `d` parameter indicates the distance threshold is now implicit in the radius values themselves, simplifying the interface and making the method work with the new coordinate representation that includes radius as a third dimension.
- `position_candidates`: `position_candidates(self, xyr_i, neighbors)`
  > Generates candidate positions by horizontally offsetting a point to avoid overlaps with neighboring points.
  This method takes a point `xyr_i` (with x, y coordinates and radius) and a list of neighboring points, then returns an array of candidate (x, y, r) coordinates where the point could be repositioned along the x-axis while maintaining its y-coordinate and radius. The method systematically computes horizontal offsets based on circular collision geometry with each neighbor, alternating left and right placements to explore valid positions. The signature was simplified from the previous version by removing the explicit distance parameter `d`, now relying on radius information embedded in the point tuples themselves, reflecting a refactoring toward more compact geometric representation in the swarm plotting algorithm.
- `first_non_overlapping_candidate`: `first_non_overlapping_candidate(self, candidates, neighbors)`
  > Finds and returns the first candidate position that does not overlap with existing swarm neighbors.
  This method iterates through a sorted list of candidate positions and returns the first one whose distance to all neighbors exceeds a non-overlapping threshold. The method handles the edge case where no neighbors exist by returning the closest candidate to the midline. It raises RuntimeError if no non-overlapping candidate can be found, ensuring the swarm placement algorithm always produces valid positions. The signature was simplified to remove the explicit distance parameter `d`, which is now inferred from the candidate and neighbor coordinate tuples that include radius information.
- `add_gutters`: `add_gutters(self, points, center)`

  This method modifies a points array in-place to prevent coordinates from extending beyond a territory defined by `center ± half_width`, where `half_width` is derived from `self.width`. ### `least_squares` (function) — `xarray/core/dask_array_ops.py`
> Solves linear least-squares problems with optional NaN handling, dispatching to dask or numpy implementations based on input type.
Signature: `least_squares(lhs, rhs, rcond=None, skipna=False)`
This function wraps least-squares fitting by delegating to either `dask_array_ops.least_squares` for dask arrays or `nputils.least_squares` for numpy arrays, supporting an optional `skipna` parameter to handle missing values. The `skipna` mode reshapes 1D right-hand sides and applies NaN masking before solving via `np.linalg.lstsq`. It returns coefficients and residuals, with tests verifying correctness on small synthetic problems and compatibility with both dense and chunked dask arrays.

### `lhs` (variable)
> A Vandermonde matrix constructed from interpolation indices and polynomial degree coordinates for polynomial fitting.
The `lhs` variable represents the left-hand side design matrix in a least-squares polynomial fitting operation, constructed using NumPy's `vander` function to generate Vandermonde matrix coefficients. It has dimensions corresponding to the coordinate being interpolated and the polynomial degree, with coordinates properly aligned for xarray operations. The matrix is later multiplied element-wise with polynomial coefficients and summed over the degree dimension to produce the fitted polynomial values, making it central to the polyfit computation pipeline that handles both regular and weighted least-squares problems.

### `residuals` (variable)
> The sum of squared residuals from a least-squares polynomial fit computation.
`residuals` captures the output of `np.linalg.lstsq` or `da.linalg.lstsq`, representing the sum of squared differences between observed and fitted values. It is extracted from the last row of the results array (or as the fourth return value) and reshaped to match the input dimensions when necessary. The variable is conditionally included in polyfit output only when `full=True` or `cov=True`, and is wrapped as a DataArray with appropriate coordinates and naming conventions for dataset integration.

### `rhs` (variable)
> The right-hand side data array or matrix used as the dependent variable in least-squares regression computations.
`rhs` represents the dependent variable (observation/target values) in a least-squares fitting operation, contrasted with `lhs` (the design matrix). It can be either a 1D or 2D array and is reshaped internally when 1D to enable consistent matrix operations. The variable is processed differently depending on the `skipna` flag: when True, NaN values are handled selectively by column; when False, standard linear algebra solvers are applied directly. It may be chunked as a Dask array for distributed computation or a NumPy array for in-memory operations.

+.. _compute.curvefit:
+
+Fitting arbitrary functions
+===========================
+
+Xarray objects also provide an interface for fitting more complex functions using
+:py:meth:`scipy.optimize.curve_fit`. :py:meth:`~xarray.DataArray.curvefit` accepts
+user-defined functions and can fit along multiple coordinates.
+
+For example, we can fit a relationship between two ``DataArray`` objects, maintaining
+a unique fit at each spatial coordinate but aggregating over the time dimension:
+
+.. ipython:: python
+
+    def exponential(x, a, xc):
+        return np.exp((x - xc) / a)
+
+
+    x = np.arange(-5, 5, 0.1)
+    t = np.arange(-5, 5, 0.1)
+    X, T = np.meshgrid(x, t)
+    Z1 = np.random.uniform(low=-5, high=5, size=X.shape)
+    Z2 = exponential(Z1, 3, X)
+    Z3 = exponential(Z1, 1, -X)
+
+    ds = xr.Dataset(
+        data_vars=dict(
+            var1=(["t", "x"], Z1), var2=(["t", "x"], Z2), var3=(["t", "x"], Z3)
+        ),
+        coords={"t": t, "x": x},
+    )
+    ds[["var2", "var3"]].curvefit(
+        coords=ds.var1,
+        func=exponential,
+        reduce_dims="t",
+        bounds={"a": (0.5, 5), "xc": (-5, 5)},
+    )
+
+We can also fit multi-dimensional functions, and even use a wrapper function to
+simultaneously fit a summation of several functions, such as this field containing
+two gaussian peaks:
+
+.. ipython:: python
+
+    def gaussian_2d(coords, a, xc, yc, xalpha, yalpha):
+        x, y = coords
+        z = a * np.exp(
+            -np.square(x - xc) / 2 / np.square(xalpha)
+            - np.square(y - yc) / 2 / np.square(yalpha)
+        )
+        return z
+
+
+    def multi_peak(coords, *args):
+        z = np.zeros(coords[0].shape)
+        for i in range(len(args) // 5):
+            z += gaussian_2d(coords, *args[i * 5 : i * 5 + 5])
+        return z
+
+
+    x = np.arange(-5, 5, 0.1)
+    y = np.arange(-5, 5, 0.1)
+    X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)
+
+    n_peaks = 2
+    names = ["a", "xc", "yc", "xalpha", "yalpha"]
+    names = [f"{name}{i}" for i in range(n_peaks) for name in names]
+    Z = gaussian_2d((X, Y), 3, 1, 1, 2, 1) + gaussian_2d((X, Y), 2, -1, -2, 1, 1)
+    Z += np.random.normal(scale=0.1, size=Z.shape)
+
+    da = xr.DataArray(Z, dims=["y", "x"], coords={"y": y, "x": x})
+    da.curvefit(
+        coords=["x", "y"],
+        func=multi_peak,
+        param_names=names,
+        kwargs={"maxfev": 10000},
+    )
+

+    This method replicates the behavior of :py:func:`scipy.optimize.curve_fit`.

### `bounds_defaults` (variable)
> A dictionary mapping parameter names to their default lower and upper bound tuples for curve fitting optimization.
`bounds_defaults` stores the valid range constraints for each parameter in a curve-fitting function, initialized to unbounded (-inf, inf) for all parameters and then updated with user-provided bounds or derived from the `bounds` argument. The dictionary is constructed alongside `param_defaults` in `_initialize_curvefit_params` and used to populate the scipy optimization bounds argument, ensuring parameters remain within specified feasible regions during fitting. It handles edge cases where default parameter values fall outside provided bounds by triggering feasible value initialization, and maintains a one-to-one correspondence with parameters throughout the curve-fitting workflow.

### `func_args` (variable)
> A dictionary mapping parameter names to their inspect.Parameter objects extracted from a function's signature.
`func_args` stores the result of `inspect.signature(func).parameters`, capturing metadata about each function parameter including default values and parameter kinds (positional, keyword, variadic). It enables downstream code to access default values via `func_args[p].default` and detect variadic parameters through `p.kind` checks. When signature inspection fails, it defaults to an empty dictionary, and callers must provide explicit `param_names` to proceed. The variable is returned alongside extracted parameter names and used by `_initialize_curvefit_params` to populate default values for curve-fitting operations.

### `p0` (variable)
> Optional dictionary mapping parameter names to initial guess values for curve fitting optimization.
The `p0` parameter accepts a dictionary where keys are parameter names and values are initial guesses passed to scipy's `curve_fit` function. When `p0` is `None` (the default), it is converted to an empty dictionary and scipy's default initialization behavior applies. The function `_initialize_curvefit_params` merges user-provided `p0` values with defaults, prioritizing explicit `p0` entries over computed feasible values derived from bounds. In the test, `p0={"n0": 4}` provides an initial guess for the "n0" parameter while allowing other parameters to use defaults.

### `param_defaults` (variable)
> A dictionary mapping parameter names to their default values, initialized from function signatures and user-provided overrides.
`param_defaults` stores the default value for each parameter in a curve-fitting function, initialized to 1 for all parameters and then updated with values from the function's signature, user-provided `p0` dictionary, and feasible values computed from bounds constraints. The dictionary ensures every parameter has a valid starting value for optimization, with bounds-constrained parameters receiving feasible initialization when their defaults fall outside the specified bounds. It is returned alongside `bounds_defaults` and used to populate the `p0` argument for scipy's curve-fitting routines.

It replaces the deprecated `fix_import_path` function, which relied on automatic package discovery, by requiring callers to explicitly provide paths obtained from `discover_package_path`. The function handles edge cases where paths already exist in sys.path (avoiding duplicates) and maintains the original order of sys.path entries, as verified by tests that check sys.path state before, during, and after context manager execution.

### `discover_package_path` (function) — `pylint/lint/expand_modules.py`
> Discovers and returns the package root directory path for a given module, respecting optional source root constraints.
Signature: `discover_package_path(modulepath: str, source_roots: Sequence[str]) -> str`
This function takes a module path (file or directory) and a sequence of source roots, then returns the real absolute path to the package directory containing that module. It normalizes the input path by expanding user home directories and resolving symlinks, handles both file and directory inputs by extracting the directory component when needed, and respects source root boundaries when provided to constrain the package discovery. The function replaces the deprecated `get_python_path` which made incorrect assumptions about `__init__.py` files always existing (invalid since PEP 420 namespace packages in Python 3.3+), and is used throughout the codebase to compute additional sys.path entries for proper module resolution.

### `extra_packages_paths` (variable)
> A sequence of filesystem paths to be added to Python's module search path during parallel linting.
`extra_packages_paths` is a parameter that receives a deduplicated sequence of directory paths discovered from input files and source roots, then passed to worker processes to augment their `sys.path`. It replaces the previous `arguments` parameter which conflated file paths with import paths. The variable is constructed by collecting unique package paths via `discover_package_path()` and used with context managers like `augmented_sys_path()` to ensure workers can import modules from the same locations as the main process, maintaining consistency between single-job and parallel execution modes.

The code checks whether a given module directory falls under each `source_root` using `os.path.commonpath()` to verify containment, returning the first matching root as the discovered source location. This variable enables explicit source root configuration as an alternative to the legacy `__init__.py` upward traversal discovery mechanism, allowing users to specify where Python modules are located rather than relying on package markers.

### `source_roots` (variable)
> A sequence of directory paths that serve as root locations for discovering Python package structures.
`source_roots` is a configuration parameter passed to `discover_package_path()` to identify candidate root directories where Python modules and packages are located. The function iterates through each source root, normalizes its path, and checks if it is a common ancestor of the target module's directory using `os.path.commonpath()`. This enables pylint to correctly identify package boundaries in non-standard project layouts, particularly for PEP 420 namespace packages where traditional package detection fails. The parameter is read from configuration files (with comma-separated values), passed through the linting pipeline, and used in test fixtures to specify custom source hierarchies.

+.. _logging:
+
+Logging
+-------
+
+.. versionadded 3.3.0
+
+.. note::
+
+   This feature is a drop-in replacement for the `pytest-catchlog
+   <https://pypi.org/project/pytest-catchlog/>`_ plugin and they will conflict
+   with each other. The backward compatibility API with ``pytest-capturelog``
+   has been dropped when this feature was introduced, so if for that reason you
+   still need ``pytest-catchlog`` you can disable the internal feature by
+   adding to your ``pytest.ini``:
+
+   .. code-block:: ini
+
+       [pytest]
+           addopts=-p no:logging
+
+Log messages are captured by default and for each failed test will be shown in
+the same manner as captured stdout and stderr.
+
+Running without options::
+
+    pytest
+
+Shows failed tests like so::
+
+    ----------------------- Captured stdlog call ----------------------
+    test_reporting.py    26 INFO     text going to logger
+    ----------------------- Captured stdout call ----------------------
+    text going to stdout
+    ----------------------- Captured stderr call ----------------------
+    text going to stderr
+    ==================== 2 failed in 0.02 seconds =====================
+
+By default each captured log message shows the module, line number, log level
+and message.  Showing the exact module and line number is useful for testing and
+debugging.  If desired the log format and date format can be specified to
+anything that the logging module supports.
+
+Running pytest specifying formatting options::
+
+    pytest --log-format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s" \
+            --log-date-format="%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"
+
+Shows failed tests like so::
+
+    ----------------------- Captured stdlog call ----------------------
+    2010-04-10 14:48:44 INFO text going to logger
+    ----------------------- Captured stdout call ----------------------
+    text going to stdout
+    ----------------------- Captured stderr call ----------------------
+    text going to stderr
+    ==================== 2 failed in 0.02 seconds =====================
+
+These options can also be customized through a configuration file:
+
+.. code-block:: ini
+
+    [pytest]
+    log_format = %(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s
+    log_date_format = %Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S
+
+Further it is possible to disable reporting logs on failed tests completely
+with::
+
+    pytest --no-print-logs
+
+Or in you ``pytest.ini``:
+
+.. code-block:: ini
+
+  [pytest]
+  log_print = False
+
+
+Shows failed tests in the normal manner as no logs were captured::
+
+    ----------------------- Captured stdout call ----------------------
+    text going to stdout
+    ----------------------- Captured stderr call ----------------------
+    text going to stderr
+    ==================== 2 failed in 0.02 seconds =====================
+
+Inside tests it is possible to change the log level for the captured log
+messages.  This is supported by the ``caplog`` fixture::
+
+    def test_foo(caplog):
+        caplog.set_level(logging.INFO)
+        pass
+
+By default the level is set on the handler used to catch the log messages,
+however as a convenience it is also possible to set the log level of any
+logger::
+
+    def test_foo(caplog):
+        caplog.set_level(logging.CRITICAL, logger='root.baz')
+        pass
+
+It is also possible to use a context manager to temporarily change the log
+level::
+
+    def test_bar(caplog):
+        with caplog.at_level(logging.INFO):
+            pass
+
+Again, by default the level of the handler is affected but the level of any
+logger can be changed instead with::
+
+    def test_bar(caplog):
+        with caplog.at_level(logging.CRITICAL, logger='root.baz'):
+            pass
+
+Lastly all the logs sent to the logger during the test run are made available on
+the fixture in the form of both the LogRecord instances and the final log text.
+This is useful for when you want to assert on the contents of a message::
+
+    def test_baz(caplog):
+        func_under_test()
+        for record in caplog.records:
+            assert record.levelname != 'CRITICAL'
+        assert 'wally' not in caplog.text
+
+For all the available attributes of the log records see the
+``logging.LogRecord`` class.
+
+You can also resort to ``record_tuples`` if all you want to do is to ensure,
+that certain messages have been logged under a given logger name with a given
+severity and message::
+
+    def test_foo(caplog):
+        logging.getLogger().info('boo %s', 'arg')
+
+        assert caplog.record_tuples == [
+            ('root', logging.INFO, 'boo arg'),
+        ]
+
+You can call ``caplog.clear()`` to reset the captured log records in a test::
+
+    def test_something_with_clearing_records(caplog):
+        some_method_that_creates_log_records()
+        caplog.clear()
+        your_test_method()
+        assert ['Foo'] == [rec.message for rec in caplog.records]
+
+Live Logs
+^^^^^^^^^
+
+By default, pytest will output any logging records with a level higher or
+equal to WARNING. In order to actually see these logs in the console you have to
+disable pytest output capture by passing ``-s``.
+
+You can specify the logging level for which log records with equal or higher
+level are printed to the console by passing ``--log-cli-level``. This setting
+accepts the logging level names as seen in python's documentation or an integer
+as the logging level num.
+
+Additionally, you can also specify ``--log-cli-format`` and
+``--log-cli-date-format`` which mirror and default to ``--log-format`` and
+``--log-date-format`` if not provided, but are applied only to the console
+logging handler.
+
+All of the CLI log options can also be set in the configuration INI file. The
+option names are:
+
+* ``log_cli_level``
+* ``log_cli_format``
+* ``log_cli_date_format``
+
+If you need to record the whole test suite logging calls to a file, you can pass
+``--log-file=/path/to/log/file``. This log file is opened in write mode which
+means that it will be overwritten at each run tests session.
+
+You can also specify the logging level for the log file by passing
+``--log-file-level``. This setting accepts the logging level names as seen in
+python's documentation(ie, uppercased level names) or an integer as the logging
+level num.
+
+Additionally, you can also specify ``--log-file-format`` and
+``--log-file-date-format`` which are equal to ``--log-format`` and
+``--log-date-format`` but are applied to the log file logging handler.
+
+All of the log file options can also be set in the configuration INI file. The
+option names are:
+
+* ``log_file``
+* ``log_file_level``
+* ``log_file_format``
+* ``log_file_date_format``

+.. _kernel_PCA:
+
+Kernel Principal Component Analysis (kPCA)
+==========================================
+
+Exact Kernel PCA
+----------------
+
+:class:`KernelPCA` is an extension of PCA which achieves non-linear
+dimensionality reduction through the use of kernels (see :ref:`metrics`). It
+has many applications including denoising, compression and structured
+prediction (kernel dependency estimation). :class:`KernelPCA` supports both
+``transform`` and ``inverse_transform``.
+
+.. figure:: ../auto_examples/decomposition/images/sphx_glr_plot_kernel_pca_001.png
+    :target: ../auto_examples/decomposition/plot_kernel_pca.html
+    :align: center
+    :scale: 75%
+
+.. topic:: Examples:
+
+    * :ref:`sphx_glr_auto_examples_decomposition_plot_kernel_pca.py`
+
+.. topic:: References:
+
+    * Kernel PCA was introduced in "Kernel principal component analysis"
+      Bernhard Schoelkopf, Alexander J. Smola, and Klaus-Robert Mueller. 1999.
+      In Advances in kernel methods, MIT Press, Cambridge, MA, USA 327-352.
+
+
+.. _kPCA_Solvers:
+
+Choice of solver for Kernel PCA
+-------------------------------
+
+While in :class:`PCA` the number of components is bounded by the number of
+features, in :class:`KernelPCA` the number of components is bounded by the
+number of samples. Many real-world datasets have large number of samples! In
+these cases finding *all* the components with a full kPCA is a waste of
+computation time, as data is mostly described by the first few components
+(e.g. ``n_components<=100``). In other words, the centered Gram matrix that
+is eigendecomposed in the Kernel PCA fitting process has an effective rank that
+is much smaller than its size. This is a situation where approximate
+eigensolvers can provide speedup with very low precision loss.
+
+The optional parameter ``eigen_solver='randomized'`` can be used to
+*significantly* reduce the computation time when the number of requested
+``n_components`` is small compared with the number of samples. It relies on
+randomized decomposition methods to find an approximate solution in a shorter
+time.
+
+The time complexity of the randomized :class:`KernelPCA` is
+:math:`O(n_{\mathrm{samples}}^2 \cdot n_{\mathrm{components}})`
+instead of :math:`O(n_{\mathrm{samples}}^3)` for the exact method
+implemented with ``eigen_solver='dense'``.
+
+The memory footprint of randomized :class:`KernelPCA` is also proportional to
+:math:`2 \cdot n_{\mathrm{samples}} \cdot n_{\mathrm{components}}` instead of
+:math:`n_{\mathrm{samples}}^2` for the exact method.
+
+Note: this technique is the same as in :ref:`RandomizedPCA`.
+
+In addition to the above two solvers, ``eigen_solver='arpack'`` can be used as
+an alternate way to get an approximate decomposition. In practice, this method
+only provides reasonable execution times when the number of components to find
+is extremely small. It is enabled by default when the desired number of
+components is less than 10 (strict) and the number of samples is more than 200
+(strict). See :class:`KernelPCA` for details.
+
